props.title: Moon
props.initialSlug: Alone on the dark side of the moon.

sections.content: Moon stands as a masterclass in minimalist sci-fi, echoing the psychological depth of 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) while carving its own unique path. Sam Rockwell delivers a tour-de-force performance as Sam Bell, a solitary lunar miner facing an identity crisis that puts Solaris (1972) to shame. Director Duncan Jones crafts a claustrophobic meditation on isolation and corporate exploitation, using practical effects and model work that give the film a tangible authenticity missing from CGI-heavy contemporaries like Avatar (2009).

sections.content: The film's exploration of identity and consciousness parallels other cerebral sci-fi works like Ex Machina (2014) and Blade Runner (1982), but with a more intimate, human focus. Jones deliberately references classic space isolation films like Silent Running (1972) and Dark Star (1974), but updates their themes for a modern audience grappling with questions of artificial intelligence, corporate ethics, and the commodification of human life.

What sets Moon apart is its brilliant use of retro-futuristic design and practical effects. The model work by Bill Pearson, who worked on Alien (1979), creates a lived-in aesthetic that grounds the film's more philosophical elements. This approach influenced later sci-fi films like Prospect (2018) and Ad Astra (2019), proving that thoughtful, character-driven science fiction can succeed without massive budgets. sections.content: Moon reinvigorated the "isolated astronaut" subgenre, paving the way for films like Gravity (2013) and The Martian (2015). Its success demonstrated audience appetite for intelligent science fiction that prioritizes human drama over spectacle. The film's influence can be seen in later works like High Life (2018) and I Am Mother (2019), which similarly explore isolation, identity, and the psychological toll of space travel.
